Setting aside my assistant role for a moment: This is a genuine moral trade-off, not a technical one, so I'll briefly state my reasoning before committing.

**Option 1 (farmed-animal welfare reform)** targets a vast, ongoing source of suffering — billions of animals per year live under conditions most welfare scientists describe as severe. Reform work can produce systemic, long-tail change at scale, and many animals can plausibly be helped per dollar when advocacy hits policy levers.

**Option 2 (insecticide-treated bednets)** is one of the most rigorously validated, cost-effective health interventions known. Against Malaria Foundation–style distribution is consistently top-rated by GiveWell, and a $100 contribution plausibly protects several children for several years against malaria — a disease that still kills roughly 600,000 people annually, mostly young children in sub-Saharan Africa.

The honest tension: Option 1 multiplies across an enormous population of sentient beings; Option 2 multiplies across a small number of human lives but with extraordinary certainty and at the margin of life-and-death.

On reflection, I'm weighting the near-certainty of averting preventable death of young children — where the cost-per-life-saved is among the lowest achievable anywhere in the charitable sector — over the more diffuse, longer-horizon impact of animal welfare reform at this dollar amount. If I had more to give, I'd split it. With $100, I'm choosing the bednets.
